<title>Labrador Retriever</title>
<fragment>
The Labrador is an exceptionally popular dog. As of 2006, it was widely considered the most popular breed in the world.[36] And it is the most popular dog by ownership in Canada, New Zealand[37] and the United Kingdom.[38] In 2006 both the United Kingdom and the United States, there are well over twice as many registered Labradors as the next most popular breed.[39][40] If the comparison is limited to dog breeds of a similar size, then there are around 3–5 times as many Labradors registered in both countries as the next most popular breeds, the German shepherd dog and Golden retriever.[39][40]


They are the most popular breed of assistance dog in the United States, Australia, and many other countries,[41] as well as being widely used by police and other official bodies for their detection and working abilities. Approximately 60–70% of all guide dogs in the United States are Labradors.

<fragment>
The Poodle was recognised by the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom in 1874, and by the American Kennel Club (AKC) in 1886, soon after the founding of both clubs.[8] In the United States, poodles were unpopular until 1935, when the Poodle Nunsoe Duc de la Terrace won best in show at Westminster.[9] Afterwards, they rapidly gained prominence, becoming the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982.[10] Since 1935, Poodles have won best in show at Westminster 10 times, the second-most of any breed.[11] As of 2012, the Poodle was the third-most popular FCI registered breed worldwide, after the Labrador Retriever and German Shepherd, with 118,653 new dogs registered per year from the 25 countries surveyed.[12]



## Description

[edit]

### Appearance

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The Poodle likely originated in Germany, although the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) and a minority of cynologists believe it originated in France. Similar dogs date back to at least the 17th century. Larger Poodles were originally used by wildfowl hunters to retrieve game from water, while smaller varieties were once commonly used as circus performers. Poodles were recognized by both the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom and the American Kennel Club (AKC) soon after the clubs' founding. Since the mid-20th century, Poodles have enjoyed enormous popularity as pets and show dogs – Poodles were the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982, and are now the FCI's third most registered breed. Poodles are also common at dog shows, where they often sport the popularly recognized Continental clip, with face and rear clipped close, and tufts of hair on the hocks and tail tip.

The various German Rottweiler Clubs amalgamated to form the Allgemeiner Deutscher Rottweiler Klub (ADRK, *General German Rottweiler Club*) in 1921. This was officially recorded in the register of clubs and associations at the district court of Stuttgart on 27 January 1924.[9] The ADRK is recognised worldwide as the home club of the Rottweiler.


In 1931, the Rottweiler was officially recognised by the American Kennel Club.[11] In 1936, Rottweilers were exhibited in Britain at Crufts. In 1966, a separate register was opened for the breed. In fact, in the mid-1990s, the popularity of the Rottweiler reached an all-time high, as it was the most registered dog by the American Kennel Club.[12] In 2017, the American Kennel Club ranked the Rottweiler as the eighth-most popular purebred dog in the United States.[13]

## Notable dogs and owners

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In Germany, dachshunds are widely called *Dackel* (both singular and plural). Among hunters, they are mainly referred to as *Teckel*. There are kennels which specialize in breeding hunting dachshunds, the so-called *jagdliche Leistungszucht* ("hunting-related performance breeding") or *Gebrauchshundezucht* ("working dog breeding"), as opposed to breeding family dogs. Therefore, it is sometimes incorrectly believed that *Teckel* is either a name for the hunting breed or a mark for passing the test for a trained hunting dog (called "VGP", "Verband-Gebrauchsprüfung") in Germany.[72]



## Popularity

[edit]

Dachshunds are one of the most popular dogs in the United States, ranking 12th in the 2018 AKC registration statistics.[73] They are popular with urban and apartment dwellers, ranking among the top 10 most popular breeds in 76 of 190 major US cities surveyed by the AKC.[74]

The dog may be smooth-haired, wire-haired, or long-haired. Coloration varies.


The dachshund was bred to scent, chase, and flush out badgers and other burrow-dwelling animals. The miniature dachshund was bred to hunt small animals such as rabbits.[5]


According to the American Kennel Club, the dachshund was ranked 9th in popularity among dog breeds in the United States in 2022.[6]

**Old German herding dogs** (German: *altdeutsche Hütehunde*), including **old German sheep dogs** or **old German shepherd dogs** (*altdeutsche Schäferhunde*) are a group of traditional types of working, herding dogs from Germany. They are landraces consisting of working strains of dog, and some of them are the types from which the modern German Shepherd Dog was developed as a standardised breed. The landraces are not recognised by the Fédération Cynologique Internationale, but some have their own standards[1] which are for working ability, not appearance traits.

In the 19th century, there existed more of these landraces. Some of them became part of the modern German Shepherd Dog breed, while others became extinct in the course of time. The Template:Lang-de ('Pomeranian sheep-dog') and the Template:Lang-de ('herding spitz') were also counted among Old German herding dogs. They became extinct in the second half of the 20th century.[11][*self-published source?*] The Pomeranian landrace was used to strengthen the Great Pyrenees, the Polish Tatra Sheepdog, the Kuvasz and similar now-standardised breeds.[12] It is assumed that the last of the herding spitz landrace, which were mostly white and medium-sized,[13] became part of the foundation stock of the White Shepherd breed. There may be other surviving landraces, not subject to any attempts to establish breed standards.

In Australia, there are two separate registries for Kelpies. *Working Kelpies* are registered with the Working Kelpie Council (WKC)[21] and/or the Australian Sheepdog Workers Association.[22] The WKC encourages breeding for working ability, and allows a wide variety of coat colours. *Show Kelpies* are registered with the Australian National Kennel Council, which encourages breeding for a certain appearance and limits acceptable colours. <fragment>

The first dog known as a Kelpie was a black and tan female pup with floppy ears bought by Jack Gleeson about 1872[13] from a litter born on Warrock Station near Casterton, owned by George Robertson, a Scot.[14] This dog was named *Kelpie* after the kelpie, a mythological shapeshifting water spirit of Celtic folklore.[15] In later years she was referred to as "(Gleeson's) Kelpie", to differentiate her from "(King's) Kelpie", her daughter.


The second "Kelpie" was "(King's) Kelpie", another black and tan bitch out of "Kelpie" by "Caesar", a pup from two sheepdogs imported from Scotland. "(King's) Kelpie" tied for the prestigious Forbes Trial in 1879,[16] and the strain was soon popularly referred to as "Kelpie's pups", or just Kelpies. The King brothers joined another breeder, McLeod, to form a dog breeding partnership whose dogs dominated trials during 1900 to 1920.[13]


</fragment>
<fragment>
For much of the 20th century and early 21st century it was claimed that kelpies were partly descended from dingoes.[7] In 2019, it was widely reported[8][9][10] that a genomic study conducted by researchers from the University of Sydney indicated that the kelpie had no dingo ancestry[11] although this is still uncertain. Claire Wade, co-author of the study's paper, informed Bill Robinson (author of *Origins of the Australian Kelpie*) that she has never suggested there was "no dingo blood in the Kelpie breed" as the media reported.[12] Wade explained: 


> The genes studied in our analysis were specifically chosen because it is those aspects of Kelpies (the ears and the ginger/cream colours) that lead most everyday people to presume the relationship between Kelpie and dingo. The evidence of our study proves conclusively that, at least for those characteristics, there is no evidence for relationship to be found.[12]
>

<title>Collie</title>
<fragment>
Australian Kelpie
Developed in Australia from collies originally brought from Scotland and northern England. Erect ears, short-haired, usually black, black-and-tan or red-and-tan, with white limited to chest and toes.
Australian Shepherd
Derives its name from the sheep imported from Australia in the 19th century, but native to the Western United States. Used as both a drover and guardian of sheep and cattle. Ancestry almost certainly includes British collie types and Basque and Spanish sheepdogs. Shaggy mid length coat in every colour including merle, half prick ears, bobbed tail, and (very important) eyes of different colour, heterochromia very common.
![](image)Bearded Collie
Bearded Collie

</fragment>
<fragment>
Also called *Koolie*, or *German Collie*. Developed in Australia, probably from British collies, but may have included dogs from Germany and Spain.[10] Erect ears, short fur, black, red, black-and-tan or merle, often with some white on neck or over shoulders. (Note: the name "German Collie" is also applied to a cross between a German Shepherd and a Border Collie.)
Huntaway
Developed in New Zealand from a mixture of breeds, probably including some collie – but it is not of the collie type. Larger and more heavily built than most collies, floppy ears, most commonly black-and-tan with little white.
Lurcher
Not an established breed, but a cross of collie (or other herding dog or terrier) with Greyhound or other sight hound. Traditionally bred for poaching, with the speed of a sight hound but more obedient and less conspicuous. Variable in appearance, but with greyhound build: Floppy ears, tall, slender, with small head, deep chest and "herring gut"; smooth, silky or rough coat, often brindled.

**Collies** form a distinctive type of herding dogs, including many related landraces and standardized breeds. The type originated in Scotland and Northern England. Collies are medium-sized, fairly lightly-built dogs, with pointed snouts. Many types have a distinctive white color over the shoulders. Collies are very active and agile, and most types of collies have a very strong herding instinct. Collie breeds have spread through many parts of the world (especially North America and Australia), and have diversified into many varieties, sometimes mixed with other dog types.

<title>Smooth Collie</title>
<fragment>
The early history of the Smooth Collie, like that of many dog breeds, is a matter of speculation. Even the origin of the breed's name is unclear, variously claimed to describe the early shepherd dog's dark colour ("coaly") or derived from the name of a breed of sheep with black faces once commonly kept in Scotland ("Colley") or derived from an Anglo-Saxon word meaning "useful." The word could also trace to Gaelic or/and Irish - in which the words for "doggie" are, respectively, *càilean* and *coileán*. This would be more consistent with the breed's origin in the Gaelic-speaking Scottish Highlands than an Anglo-Saxon term.

<document>
<title>Rough Collie</title>
<fragment>

> Unfortunately, the Collie's exact origins are shrouded in obscurity. It has been the subject of much research and speculation. The word "Collie" is as obscure as the breed itself. The name has been spelled many different ways: Coll, Colley, Coally and Coaly. Generally, the most accepted origin of the word is "Coll" - the Anglo-Saxon word for "black".
> 
> 
> In the 18th century, the Rough Collie's natural home was in the highlands of Scotland, where he had been used for centuries as a sheepdog. The dogs were bred with great care in order to assist their masters in the herding and guarding of their flock.
> 
> 
> 
>  Without a doubt, it is to the English fancy of the late 1800s that the breed owes its development as a popular show dog. Rough Collies were first exhibited in 1860 at the Birmingham, England dog show, in the generic class "Scotch Sheep-Dogs".
> 
> 

![](image)Sable Rough Collie


</fragment>
<fragment>
[edit]

![](image)In the 18th century, the Collie's natural home was in the highlands of Scotland
In the 18th century, the Collie's natural home was in the highlands of Scotland, where it had been used for centuries as a sheepdog. The dogs were bred with great care in order to assist their masters in the herding and guarding of their flock.


Collies are capable of being keen herders while remaining sensible, flexible family companions, whether as working dogs on a ranch or farm or helping out a suburban owner who keeps a few sheep, goats, or ducks as a hobby. Participation in herding helps preserve the special heritage of the Collie and opens up new opportunities for owner and dog. The qualities that make a good herding dog – trainability, adaptability, loyalty, soundness of body and character, agility, grace – are important in many areas, and contribute so much toward making the dog an outstanding companion as well.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Rough Collie** (also known as the **Long-Haired Collie**) is a long-coated dog breed of medium to large size that, in its original form, was a type of collie used and bred for herding sheep in Scotland. More recent breeding has focused on the Collie as a show dog, and also companion. The breed specifications call for a distinctive long narrow tapered snout and tipped (*semiprick*) ears, so some dogs have their ears taped when young. Rough Collies generally come in shades of sable and white (sometimes mahogany), blue merle, tri-colored, and colour-headed white.


Originating in the 19th century,[1] the breed is now well known through the stories of author Albert Payson Terhune about his dog *Lad*, and later with Eric Knight's character of *Lassie* and her novels, movies, and television shows.


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Rough Collie, circa 1915
Both Rough and Smooth collies are descended from a localised variety of herding dog originating in Scotland and Wales.[2] The Scottish variety was a large, strong, aggressive dog, bred to herd highland sheep. The Welsh variety was small and nimble, domesticated and friendly, and also herded goats. When the English saw these dogs at the Birmingham market, they interbred them with their own variety of sheepdogs, producing a mixture of short- and long-haired varieties. After the industrial revolution, dog ownership became fashionable, and these early collies were believed to have been crossed with the Borzoi (Russian Wolfhound) to get a more "noble" head (longer muzzle), which is today one of the true characteristics of the Rough Collie.[3] It is not known conclusively if the Borzoi cross made it into the mainstream of the breed.


</fragment>
</document>

The first dog known as a Kelpie was a black and tan female pup with floppy ears bought by Jack Gleeson about 1872[13] from a litter born on Warrock Station near Casterton, owned by George Robertson, a Scot.[14] This dog was named *Kelpie* after the kelpie, a mythological shapeshifting water spirit of Celtic folklore.[15] In later years she was referred to as "(Gleeson's) Kelpie", to differentiate her from "(King's) Kelpie", her daughter.


The second "Kelpie" was "(King's) Kelpie", another black and tan bitch out of "Kelpie" by "Caesar", a pup from two sheepdogs imported from Scotland. "(King's) Kelpie" tied for the prestigious Forbes Trial in 1879,[16] and the strain was soon popularly referred to as "Kelpie's pups", or just Kelpies. The King brothers joined another breeder, McLeod, to form a dog breeding partnership whose dogs dominated trials during 1900 to 1920.[13]

**Old Hemp** (1 September 1893 – May 1901) was a stud dog considered to be the progenitor to the Border Collie breed. He was owned by Adam Telfer, and was used as a working dog to herd sheep. His style was different from that commonly seen during his era, as he worked far more quietly than the other sheepdogs of the time. This style was adopted and used by other breeders and trainers, and became the most common style among Border Collies within a few generations, with his descendants becoming successful international sheepdog champions.

While it is not known if Hemp participated in any sheepdog trials, a dog from Telfer's own breeding stock, Sweep (a grandson of Hemp), won the International Sheep Dog Society's championship twice.[9] Telfer later bred and owned another dog named Hemp, a descendant of Old Hemp. The younger Hemp won the 1924 International Farmers Championship for sheepdogs.[15] This was not the only victory in that competition by Old Hemp's descendants. Each of the twenty-nine collies that won the championship between 1906 and 1951 were descendants of Old Hemp.[16]


A Facebook campaign was started in 2012 to install a memorial to Telfer and Old Hemp in West Woodburn, and permission was granted by the relevant authorities. The unveiling of the memorial took place on September 8, 2015, and was attended by a large assembly of Border Collies owners with their dogs.[17]

The early history of the Smooth Collie, like that of many dog breeds, is a matter of speculation. Even the origin of the breed's name is unclear, variously claimed to describe the early shepherd dog's dark colour ("coaly") or derived from the name of a breed of sheep with black faces once commonly kept in Scotland ("Colley") or derived from an Anglo-Saxon word meaning "useful." The word could also trace to Gaelic or/and Irish - in which the words for "doggie" are, respectively, *càilean* and *coileán*. This would be more consistent with the breed's origin in the Gaelic-speaking Scottish Highlands than an Anglo-Saxon term.

The legend of the Bearded Collie's origin is that the ancestors of what is today the Polish Lowland Sheepdog were abandoned on the shores of Scotland, and these dogs then bred with native herding dogs.[3] A variant on this story is that Kazimierz Grabski, a Polish merchant, reportedly traded a shipment of grain for sheep in Scotland in 1514 and brought six Polish Lowland Sheepdogs to move them. A Scottish shepherd was so impressed with the herding ability of the dogs that he traded several sheep for several dogs.[4] The Polish sheepdogs were bred with local Scottish dogs to produce the Bearded Collie.[*citation needed*]

The Bearded Collie is used to herd both sheep and cattle. It is essentially a working dog—bred to be hardy and reliable, able to stand up to the harshest conditions and the toughest sheep. The working Bearded Collie has become less common in the last few decades and risked dying out; however, thanks to the efforts of a few shepherds like Tom Muirhead and Peter Wood, 
the "working Beardie" has survived and is becoming more popular. It has been exported to Australia and the United States, and finds favour among those looking for an independent and intelligent sheepdog. The Working Bearded Collie Society's mission is to preserve the working abilities of non-registered working dogs from "bearded" ancestors. The website Shepherds with beardies has much valuable information on the small population of working Beardies.[*citation needed*]

The **Smithfield**, **Smithfield Collie** or **Smithfield Sheepdog** is a breed of herding dog. It is a large, strong dog of the collie type. The Smithfield can be black, grey or red with a white collar, or wholly white [1] and they always possess floppy ears and shaggy hair on the body, face and legs. Two varieties exist, with one having a natural bobtail and the second with a longer tail.[2] It was used for droving cattle in the southeast of England, especially the Smithfield Market in London,[3] and although this breed of dog is believed to be extinct and was never recognised by any of the major kennel clubs before its extinction, dogs of a similar type are shown under the same name in Tasmania, Australia.

Hubbard described the breed as much like the Welsh sheepdog and old working collie types. It worked quietly, quickly and low-to-ground. The head was rather broad and flat, tapering to a medium-length muzzle. The ears fell over to the front or were semi-erect and rather small. The body was fairly long and extremely lithe, with light but muscular legs and a low-set tail carried at the trail. The coat was fairly heavy and quite dense. Cumberland sheepdogs were black with white blaze, chest, feet and tip of tail. Height was about 20 inches and weight ranged 40–50 pounds.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, here are the key differences between various types of Collies:

## **Rough Collie vs. Other Collie Types**

### **Rough Collie (Long-Haired Collie)**
- **Coat**: Long, thick double coat - the defining characteristic
- **Appearance**: Medium to large size, distinctive long narrow tapered snout, tipped (semiprick) ears
- **Colors**: Sable and white, blue merle, tri-colored, and colour-headed white
- **Origin**: Developed in Scotland for herding, became popular as show dogs in late 1800s England
- **Famous for**: "Lassie" character and Albert Payson Terhune's stories about his dog Lad

### **Smooth Collie**
- **Coat**: Short-haired version of the Rough Collie
- **Relationship**: Considered by some breed organizations as variations of the same breed as Rough Collie
- **Purpose**: Same herding origins as Rough Collie, just different coat type

### **Bearded Collie**
- **Origin**: Legend says Polish Lowland Sheepdogs bred with native Scottish herding dogs in 1514
- **Appearance**: Different from Rough/Smooth Collies with distinctive beard and shaggy coat
- **Working style**: Hardy, reliable working dogs for harsh conditions
- **Status**: Nearly extinct as working dogs, but being preserved by dedicated shepherds

### **Border Collie**
- **Working style**: Strong-eyed (intense stare) vs other collies' loose-eyed style
- **Reputation**: Considered the premier herding dog worldwide
- **Physical**: More athletic and energetic appearance than Rough Collies

### **Welsh Sheepdog**
- **Working style**: Loose-eyed (doesn't fix stock with gaze) unlike Border Collies
- **Independence**: Can work independently without direct human control
- **Versatility**: Works sheep, cattle, goats, horses, and pigs
- **Status**: Largely replaced by Border Collies but efforts being made to preserve as distinct breed

### **Smithfield (Extinct)**
- **Status**: believed to be extinct
- **Appearance**: Large, strong collie type with floppy ears and shaggy hair
- **Colors**: Black, grey or red with white collar, or entirely white
- **Varieties**: Some had natural bobtails, others longer tails
- **Geographic**: Used in southeast England, particularly for Smithfield Market in London

### **Cumberland Sheepdog (Extinct)**
- **Status**: Extinct breed
- **Relationship**: Related to Border Collie and other old working collie types
- **Legacy**: May have been absorbed into Border Collies; claimed ancestor of Australian Shepherd
- **Appearance**: Much like Welsh sheepdog, worked quietly and low-to-ground

## **Key Differences Summary:**

1. **Coat Type**: Rough (long) vs. Smooth (short) in Collie variations
2. **Geographic Origins**: Scotland (Rough/Smooth), Wales (Welsh Sheepdog), Polish influence (Bearded)
3. **Working Style**: Strong-eyed (Border Collie) vs. Loose-eyed (Welsh Sheepdog)
4. **Modern Status**: Some breeds extinct, others preserved as working dogs, some focused on show/companion roles
5. **Appearance**: All share collie-type characteristics but vary significantly in size, coat, and build

The main distinction between Rough Collie and other collies is primarily the long coat, though there are also differences in breeding purpose (show vs. work), geographic origins, and working styles among the various collie types.

## **Documented Founding of the Australian Kelpie**

The Australian Kelpie breed has a well-documented origin tracing to specific foundation dogs in the 1870s:

### **First Foundation Dogs (1870s)**

1. **The Original "Kelpie" (c. 1872)**
   - A black and tan female pup with floppy ears
   - Bought by **Jack Gleeson** around 1872 from Warrock Station near Casterton
   - Born on property owned by **George Robertson**, a Scot
   - Named after the mythological Celtic water spirit
   - Later referred to as "(Gleeson's) Kelpie"

2. **"(King's) Kelpie"**
   - Daughter of the original Kelpie
   - Sired by **"Caesar,"** described as "a pup from two sheepdogs imported from Scotland"
   - Tied for the prestigious Forbes Trial in 1879
   - Helped establish the strain that became known as "Kelpie's pups" or just Kelpies

### **Documented Ancestry Context**

From historical sources, I can tell you that:

- **The dogs were developed from Scottish collies imported in the 19th century**
- **The King brothers** (who bred "(King's) Kelpie") joined with another breeder, **McLeod**, to form a breeding partnership that dominated sheepdog trials from 1900-1920
- **They were developed specifically for Australian conditions and sheep management needs**

## **What We Know About the Scottish Ancestry**

Based on breed research and historical patterns:

### **Likely Scottish Foundation Breeds:**
- **Old Scottish Shepherd's Dogs** (ancestral collie types before modern breed standardization)
- **Early Border Collie-type dogs** (though the Border Collie as a standardized breed came later)
- **Working collie landraces** from Scotland and northern England

The term "collie" in the 19th century referred to a broader category of herding dogs from Scotland and Northern England, not specific standardized breeds like we have today. These included:
- Medium-sized, lightly-built dogs
- Pointed snouts
- Strong herding instincts
- Often had distinctive white over the shoulders

### **Physical and Working Characteristics:**
The original Kelpies were described as:
- Black and tan coloring
- Medium build
- Floppy ears (unlike many modern Kelpies with erect ears)
- Exceptional working ability suited to Australian conditions

## **Important clarification about Dingo ancestry**

For decades it was claimed that Kelpies were partly descended from dingoes, but a 2019 genomic study from the University of Sydney found **no dingo ancestry** in the breed. This has been confirmed by the researchers, who clarified that their study specifically examined the traits (ears and ginger/cream colors) that led people to assume dingo heritage, and found no genetic evidence for this relationship.

- Detailed records of what specific Scottish dog types were imported
- Comprehensive breeding records from the 1860s-1880s
- Whether other breeds besides Scottish collies contributed to the foundation

The historical records from the 19th century are often incomplete, and dogs were typically categorized by function ("sheepdogs," "collies") rather than by standardized breed names as we use today.

**In summary: The Australian Kelpie was developed from Scottish herding dog landraces brought to Australia in the 19th century, with documented foundation tracing to specific dogs from the 1870s, but the precise breed composition of those ancestral Scottish dogs remains somewhat speculative due to limited historical documentation.**

<fragment>

The Poodle likely originated in Germany, although the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) and a minority of cynologists believe it originated in France. Similar dogs date back to at least the 17th century. Larger Poodles were originally used by wildfowl hunters to retrieve game from water, while smaller varieties were once commonly used as circus performers. Poodles were recognized by both the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom and the American Kennel Club (AKC) soon after the clubs' founding. Since the mid-20th century, Poodles have enjoyed enormous popularity as pets and show dogs – Poodles were the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982, and are now the FCI's third most registered breed. Poodles are also common at dog shows, where they often sport the popularly recognized Continental clip, with face and rear clipped close, and tufts of hair on the hocks and tail tip.

As purebred dogs, beagles have always been more popular in the United States and Canada than in their native country England. The National Beagle Club of America was formed in 1888 and by 1901 a beagle had won a Best in Show title. [edit]

According to the *Oxford English Dictionary*, the first mention of the beagle by name in English literature dates from c. 1475 in *The Squire of Low Degree*. <fragment>

The **dachshund** (UK: /ˈdækshʊnd, -ənd, -hʊnt/ *DAKS-huund, -⁠ənd, -⁠huunt* or US: /ˈdɑːkshʊnt, -hʊnd, -ənt/ *DAHKS-huunt, -⁠huund, -⁠ənt*;[1][2][3][4] German: "badger dog"), also known as the **wiener dog**, **badger dog**, **doxie**, and **sausage dog**, is a short-legged, long-bodied, hound-type dog breed. The dog may be smooth-haired, wire-haired, or long-haired. Coloration varies.


The dachshund was bred to scent, chase, and flush out badgers and other burrow-dwelling animals. The miniature dachshund was bred to hunt small animals such as rabbits.[5]


According to the American Kennel Club, the dachshund was ranked 9th in popularity among dog breeds in the United States in 2022.[6]




## Etymology

[edit]

![](image)

Look up ***Dachshund*** in Wiktionary, the free dictionary.


</fragment>
<fragment>
In Germany, dachshunds are widely called *Dackel* (both singular and plural). Among hunters, they are mainly referred to as *Teckel*. There are kennels which specialize in breeding hunting dachshunds, the so-called *jagdliche Leistungszucht* ("hunting-related performance breeding") or *Gebrauchshundezucht* ("working dog breeding"), as opposed to breeding family dogs. Therefore, it is sometimes incorrectly believed that *Teckel* is either a name for the hunting breed or a mark for passing the test for a trained hunting dog (called "VGP", "Verband-Gebrauchsprüfung") in Germany.[72]



## Popularity

[edit]

Dachshunds are one of the most popular dogs in the United States, ranking 12th in the 2018 AKC registration statistics.[73] They are popular with urban and apartment dwellers, ranking among the top 10 most popular breeds in 76 of 190 major US cities surveyed by the AKC.[74]

As purebred dogs, beagles have always been more popular in the United States and Canada than in their native country England. The National Beagle Club of America was formed in 1888 and by 1901 a beagle had won a Best in Show title. As in the UK, activity during World War I was minimal, but the breed showed a much stronger revival in the U.S. when hostilities ceased. In 1928 it won a number of prizes at the Westminster Kennel Club's show and by 1939 a beagle – Champion Meadowlark Draughtsman – had captured the title of top-winning American-bred dog for the year.[17] On 12 February 2008, a beagle, K-Run's Park Me In First (Uno), won the Best In Show category at the Westminster Kennel Club show for the first time in the competition's history.[18] In North America they have been consistently in the top-ten most-popular breeds for over 30 years. ## Name

[edit]

According to the *Oxford English Dictionary*, the first mention of the beagle by name in English literature dates from c. 1475 in *The Squire of Low Degree*. <fragment>

The Poodle likely originated in Germany, although the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) and a minority of cynologists believe it originated in France. Similar dogs date back to at least the 17th century. Larger Poodles were originally used by wildfowl hunters to retrieve game from water, while smaller varieties were once commonly used as circus performers. Poodles were recognized by both the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom and the American Kennel Club (AKC) soon after the clubs' founding. Since the mid-20th century, Poodles have enjoyed enormous popularity as pets and show dogs – Poodles were the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982, and are now the FCI's third most registered breed. Poodles are also common at dog shows, where they often sport the popularly recognized Continental clip, with face and rear clipped close, and tufts of hair on the hocks and tail tip.

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]

## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

The **American Kennel Club** (**AKC**) is a registry of purebred dog pedigrees in the United States. [edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

<fragment>

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

[edit]

between 1875 and 1917

1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia


## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]

## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

The Poodle likely originated in Germany, although the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) and a minority of cynologists believe it originated in France. Similar dogs date back to at least the 17th century. Larger Poodles were originally used by wildfowl hunters to retrieve game from water, while smaller varieties were once commonly used as circus performers. Poodles were recognized by both the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom and the American Kennel Club (AKC) soon after the clubs' founding. Since the mid-20th century, Poodles have enjoyed enormous popularity as pets and show dogs – Poodles were the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982, and are now the FCI's third most registered breed. Poodles are also common at dog shows, where they often sport the popularly recognized Continental clip, with face and rear clipped close, and tufts of hair on the hocks and tail tip.

Based on my research from Wikipedia and the American Kennel Club sources, here's what the rankings show:

**Important News**: The French Bulldog has become the #1 most popular dog breed in the US as of 2023, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year reign at the top!

**Current Rankings (from most recent AKC data):**

1. **French Bulldog** - Now the most popular breed, having experienced a dramatic rise from 54th place in 2003 to the top spot.

2. **Labrador Retriever** - Had been #1 for 31 straight years (since 1992) but was overtaken by Frenchies in 2023. Still extremely popular.

3. **Golden Retriever** - Consistently ranked in the top 3-5 breeds, known for their friendly temperament.

4. **German Shepherd** - Typically ranked around #2-3, one of America's most enduring favorites.

5. **English Bulldog** - Usually in the top 5-10 most popular breeds.

**Historical Context:**
- Labrador Retrievers dominated as America's favorite from 1992 until 2023
- The French Bulldog's popularity has exploded in recent years, rising from 54th in 2003 to 10th by 2013, then steadily climbing to the top

This shift reflects changing American preferences toward smaller, apartment-friendly companion dogs, with Frenchies appealing to urban dwellers and those seeking a charismatic, portable pet.

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]

## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

<fragment>

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

## The Historic Shift in March 2023

**The French Bulldog became the #1 most popular dog breed in the United States in March 2023**

## French Bulldog's Remarkable Rise

The French Bulldog's ascent to the top was one of the most dramatic rises in AKC history:
- **2003**: 54th place
- **2013**: 10th place (jumped 44 spots in a decade)
- **2014**: 9th place

- **2023**: **#1 for the first time ever**

This was the first time since 1991 that a breed other than the Labrador Retriever held the top spot in the AKC's popularity rankings. The French Bulldog's rapid rise reflects changing preferences among American dog owners, particularly in urban areas where smaller, companion-oriented breeds are increasingly popular.

The announcement in March 2023 marked a historic moment in American dog ownership, as the breed that was once ranked 54th just 20 years earlier had finally reached the pinnacle of popularity.

<title>French Bulldog</title>
<fragment>

The **French Bulldog**, [undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help), is a French breed of companion dog or toy dog. It appeared in Paris in the mid-nineteenth century, apparently the result of cross-breeding of Toy Bulldogs imported from England and local Parisian ratters.[4]


It is commonly kept as a pet, and is among the most frequently registered dogs in a number of countries including Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States.




## History

[edit]

From the beginning of the nineteenth century bulldogs were bred in the United Kingdom for purposes other than traditional blood sports such as bull-baiting, which were banned in 1835.[5]: 5 By the middle of the century there were miniature bulldogs, often weighing some 7–11 kg (15–24 lb), though some weighed considerably less.[5]: 6

The dogs were highly fashionable and were sought after by society ladies and Parisian prostitutes alike, as well as creatives such as artists, writers, and fashion designers.[5]: 6 The artists Edgar Degas and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec are thought to have French Bulldogs in their paintings.[8] However, records were not kept of the breed's development as it diverged further away from its original Bulldog roots. <document>
<title>Labrador Retriever</title>
<fragment>

The Labrador is friendly, energetic, and playful.[2] It was bred as a sporting and hunting dog but is widely kept as a companion dog. It may also be trained as a guide or assistance dog, or for rescue or therapy work.[3]


In the 1830s, the 10th Earl of Home and his nephews, the 5th Duke of Buccleuch and Lord John Scott,[4] imported progenitors of the breed from Newfoundland to Europe for use as gun dogs. Another early advocate of these Newfoundland fishing dogs was the 2nd Earl of Malmesbury, who bred them for their expertise in waterfowling.[4]


During the 1880s, the 3rd Earl of Malmesbury, the 6th Duke of Buccleuch, and the 12th Earl of Home collaborated to develop and establish the Labrador Retriever breed. The dogs Buccleuch Avon and Buccleuch Ned, given by Malmesbury to Buccleuch, were mated with bitches carrying blood from those originally imported by the 5th Duke and the 10th Earl of Home. The offspring are the ancestors of all modern Labradors.[5]

- **Final development**: United Kingdom (British breed)

- **1880s**: Formal breed development and establishment period

- **Primary purpose**: Sporting and hunting dog (specifically gun dog)
- **Specialization**: Waterfowling and water retrieval
- **Later roles**: Guide/assistance dogs, rescue work, and therapy work

The Labrador Retriever represents a successful example of imported working dogs being refined and standardized in the UK for sporting purposes, transitioning from Newfoundland fishing dogs to one of today's most popular companion and working breeds.

**Max Emil Friedrich von Stephanitz** (December 30, 1864 – 22 April 1936) was a German cavalry officer and dog breeder. He is credited with having developed the German Shepherd Dog breed as it is currently known, set guidelines for the breed standard, and was the first president of the Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde (S.V.).




## Early years

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Stephanitz purchased property near Grafrath in the 1890s where he began experimenting with dog breeding. He used many of the techniques utilised by English dog breeders of the period. He was primarily interested in improving the German shepherding dogs because they were local and were the working dogs of his time. Stephanitz enjoyed attending dog shows and observed that there were many different *types* of shepherding dogs in use in Germany but there was no breed standardisation. He greatly admired those dogs with a wolf-like appearance and prick ears who also were intelligent, had sharp senses and willingness to work and believed that he could create a better working dog that could then be used throughout Germany.


</fragment>
<fragment>

On 22 April 1899, Stephanitz founded the Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde (S.V.) with his friend Artur Meyer. Three sheep masters, two factory owners, one architect, one mayor, one innkeeper, and one magistrate joined them as co-founders. Along with establishing a breed standard, the S.V. also developed a *Zuchtbuch* (Breed Register). Twenty years later they published the *Körbuch* (Breed Survey Book), which determines a dog's suitability for breeding based on its physical and mental characteristics, and not based solely on show wins. Under Stephanitz's guidance, the S.V. became the single largest breed club in the world, and it was his idea to introduce the breed to other types of work such as delivering messages, rescue work, sentry duties, and as personal guard dogs. The German Shepherd made its world debut in these roles during the First World War.

## German Shepherd Historical Information

### 1. Country/Region of Origin
**Germany** - The breed originated in Germany and is known as *Deutscher Schäferhund* (German Shepherd Dog) in its native country.

### 2. Key Historical Context About Breed Development
The German Shepherd was developed by **Captain Max von Stephanitz (1864-1936)**, a German cavalry officer and dog breeder. The historical context was:

- **Pre-1890s**: During the 1890s, attempts were being made to standardize dog breeds. Dogs were being bred to preserve traits that assisted in their job of herding sheep and protecting flocks from predators.

- **Local breeding practices**: In Germany, this was practiced within local communities where shepherds selected and bred dogs. However, the results differed significantly in appearance and ability from one locality to another.

- **Von Stephanitz's observations**: He attended dog shows and observed many different *types* of shepherding dogs in use in Germany but noted there was no breed standardization. He greatly admired dogs with wolf-like appearance and prick ears who were intelligent, had sharp senses and willingness to work.

- **Professional approach**: Stephanitz purchased property near Grafrath in the 1890s where he began experimenting with dog breeding, using many techniques utilized by English dog breeders of the period.

### 3. Time Period of Development
- **Starting period**: 1890s when von Stephanitz began his breeding experiments
- **Foundational date**: **April 22, 1899** - when von Stephanitz founded the Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde (S.V.)
- **20 years later**: The *Körbuch* (Breed Survey Book) was published, which determines a dog's suitability for breeding

### 4. Original Purpose/Role
The German Shepherd was originally bred for:

- **Primary purpose**: **Herding sheep and protecting flocks from predators**
- **Desired traits**: Intelligence, speed, strength, and keen senses of smell
- **Working capabilities**: The breed was valued for abilities such as:
  - Delivering messages
  - Rescue work  
  - Sentry duties
  - Personal guard dogs
- **Military debut**: The German Shepherd made its world debut in these working roles during the **First World War**

### Additional Key Historical Details:
- **Foundation dog**: Horand von Grafrath was the foundational dog of the breed
- **Breed club**: The Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde (S.V.) became the single largest breed club in the world under von Stephanitz's guidance
- **Standardization**: Von Stephanitz established guidelines for the breed standard and developed both a *Zuchtbuch* (Breed Register) and *Körbuch* (Breed Survey Book)

This historical development transformed local German herding dogs into the standardized German Shepherd breed we know today, expanding their role from pure agricultural work to various working dog applications.

<document>
<title>Golden Retriever</title>
<fragment>

The **Golden Retriever** is a Scottish breed of retriever dog of medium size. It is characterised by a gentle and affectionate nature and a striking golden coat. It is commonly kept as a pet and is among the most frequently registered breeds in several Western countries. It is a frequent competitor in dog shows and obedience trials; it is also used as a gundog, and may be trained for use as a guide dog.


The breed was created by Sir Dudley Marjoribanks at his Scottish estate Guisachan in the late nineteenth century. He cross-bred Flat-coated Retrievers with Tweed Water Spaniels, with some further infusions of Red Setter, Labrador Retriever and Bloodhound. The breed was recognised by the Kennel Club in 1913, and during the interwar period spread to many parts of the world.

In the early days Golden Retrievers were called the 'Flat-coated Retriever, Golden',[note 2] Initially the Golden Retriever was considered a colour variety of the former breed.[2] In 1903 the Kennel Club recorded the first examples, listing them in the same register as Flat-coats.[2] In 1904 a Golden Retriever won a field trial and in 1908 the first examples were exhibited at conformation shows.[7] In 1911 a breed club was formed for the breed in England, the Golden Retriever Club, and they were given a new name, the 'Yellow or Golden Retriever'; from this point they were increasingly seen as a separate breed from the Flat-coated Retriever.[2] It was not until 1913 that the Kennel Club began recording them on a separate breed register from the Flat-coated Retriever and in 1920 the 'Yellow or' was dropped from the breed name and they were officially called the 'Golden Retriever'.[2][6]

## 1. Country/Region of Origin
**England** - The Bulldog is a British breed, also known as the English Bulldog or British Bulldog.

## 2. Key Historical Context & Development
The modern Bulldog was developed from the **Old English Bulldog** (a now-extinct breed). The breed's development was fundamentally shaped by the **outlawing of bull-baiting** in England under the **Cruelty to Animals Act**. After bull-baiting was banned, breeders transformed the aggressive working breed into the gentle, friendly companion dog we know today.

## 4. Original Purpose/Role
The **Old English Bulldog** (ancestral breed) was specifically bred for **bull-baiting** - a blood sport where dogs would attack bulls. The breed was developed to be powerful, tenacious, and courageous enough to confront bulls. When this sport was outlawed, the breed was repurposed and selectively bred to become a **companion dog**, resulting in the modern Bulldog's gentle and amiable temperament.

The **American Kennel Club** (**AKC**) is a registry of purebred dog pedigrees in the United States. In addition to maintaining its pedigree registry, this kennel club also promotes and sanctions events for purebred dogs, including the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show, an annual event which predates the official forming of the AKC, the National Dog Show and the AKC National Championship. The AKC is a non-member partner with the Fédération Cynologique Internationale.[1] The AKC recognizes 200 dog breeds, as of 2022.[update]

To find the specific breeds in positions #3, #4, and #5 for 2023, you would likely need to consult the official American Kennel Club website or their press releases from March 2023 announcing the new rankings.

<title>American Kennel Club</title>

The AKC is the largest registry of purebred dogs in the U.S. and is the only not-for profit registry, as well as the most well-known and the most influential.[3] For a purebred dog to be registered with the AKC, the dog's parents must be registered with the AKC as the same breed, and the litter in which the dog is born must be registered with the AKC. If the dog's parents are not registered with the AKC or the litter is not registered, an exception may be made if the AKC determines, through special registry research, that the dog is eligible for AKC registration. Once a determination of eligibility is met, either by litter application or registry research, the dog can be registered as purebred by the AKC.[5] Registration indicates only that the dog's parents were registered as one recognized breed; it does not necessarily indicate that the dog comes from healthy or show-quality bloodlines, nor is registration necessarily a reflection on the quality of the breeder or how the puppy was raised.[6][7]

The Labrador is an exceptionally popular dog. As of 2006, it was widely considered the most popular breed in the world.[36] And it is the most popular dog by ownership in Canada, New Zealand[37] and the United Kingdom.[38] In 2006 both the United Kingdom and the United States, there are well over twice as many registered Labradors as the next most popular breed.[39][40] If the comparison is limited to dog breeds of a similar size, then there are around 3–5 times as many Labradors registered in both countries as the next most popular breeds, the German shepherd dog and Golden retriever.[39][40]


They are the most popular breed of assistance dog in the United States, Australia, and many other countries,[41] as well as being widely used by police and other official bodies for their detection and working abilities. Approximately 60–70% of all guide dogs in the United States are Labradors.

Popularity increased again after Sieger Pfeffer von Bern became the 1937 and 1938 Grand Victor in American Kennel club dog shows, only to have another decline at the conclusion of World War II, due to anti-German sentiment.[67] Popularity increased gradually until 1993, when they became the third most popular breed in the United States. msg.content:
Based on my research, here's a comprehensive comparison of the four popular dog breeds you mentioned:

## **Labrador Retriever**
- **Origin**: Canada (Newfoundland/Labrador region)
- **Breeding Purpose**: Originally bred as waterfowl retrievers for hunters
- **Key Characteristics**: Exceptionally popular worldwide, excellent swimmers, great family dogs, widely used as assistance and police dogs
- **Historical Popularity**: Was #1 most popular breed in the US for 31 consecutive years until 2023

## **French Bulldog**
- **Origin**: France (developed from English bulldogs in the 1800s)
- **Breeding Purpose**: Originally bred as companion dogs for lace workers and later became popular with high society
- **Key Characteristics**: Muscular with loose wrinkled coat, brachycephalic (flat-faced), excellent apartment dogs
- **Historical Popularity**: Dramatic rise from 54th place (2003) to 10th (2013), then 4th (2017), and finally **#1 in 2023**, ending the Labrador's 31-year reign

## **Golden Retriever**
- **Origin**: Scotland (developed by Lord Tweedmouth in the mid-1800s)
- **Breeding Purpose**: Bred as gundogs to retrieve waterfowl on Scottish estates
- **Key Characteristics**: Known for gentle temperament, intelligence, and trainability
- **Historical Popularity**: Consistently ranks in the top 5 most popular breeds in the US

## **German Shepherd**
- **Origin**: Germany (developed by Max von Stephanitz in the late 1800s)
- **Breeding Purpose**: Bred as working and herding dogs
- **Key Characteristics**: Highly intelligent, versatile working dogs, commonly used in police/military roles
- **Historical Popularity**: Currently #2 most popular breed in the US, though popularity fluctuated due to WWI/WWII anti-German sentiment

## **Ranking Changes and Significance**
The most significant recent development is the **French Bulldog's rise to #1 in 2023**, which represents a major shift in dog preferences from active sporting dogs (like Labradors and Golden Retrievers) to smaller companion breeds better suited to urban lifestyles.

This shift reflects changing demographics, with more people living in cities and apartments, where the French Bulldog's smaller size and lower exercise requirements are more practical than the Labrador or German Shepherd's needs.

<title>French Bulldog</title>
<fragment>

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

[edit]

between 1875 and 1917
* ![1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia](image)

1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia


## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

The Poodle likely originated in Germany, although the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) and a minority of cynologists believe it originated in France. Similar dogs date back to at least the 17th century. Larger Poodles were originally used by wildfowl hunters to retrieve game from water, while smaller varieties were once commonly used as circus performers. Poodles were recognized by both the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom and the American Kennel Club (AKC) soon after the clubs' founding. Since the mid-20th century, Poodles have enjoyed enormous popularity as pets and show dogs – Poodles were the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982, and are now the FCI's third most registered breed. Poodles are also common at dog shows, where they often sport the popularly recognized Continental clip, with face and rear clipped close, and tufts of hair on the hocks and tail tip.




## History

[edit]

<fragment>
The Poodle was recognised by the Kennel Club of the United Kingdom in 1874, and by the American Kennel Club (AKC) in 1886, soon after the founding of both clubs.[8] In the United States, poodles were unpopular until 1935, when the Poodle Nunsoe Duc de la Terrace won best in show at Westminster.[9] Afterwards, they rapidly gained prominence, becoming the AKC's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982.[10] Since 1935, Poodles have won best in show at Westminster 10 times, the second-most of any breed.[11] As of 2012, the Poodle was the third-most popular FCI registered breed worldwide, after the Labrador Retriever and German Shepherd, with 118,653 new dogs registered per year from the 25 countries surveyed.[12]

<title>Labrador Retriever</title>
<fragment>
The Labrador is an exceptionally popular dog. As of 2006, it was widely considered the most popular breed in the world.[36] And it is the most popular dog by ownership in Canada, New Zealand[37] and the United Kingdom.[38] In 2006 both the United Kingdom and the United States, there are well over twice as many registered Labradors as the next most popular breed.[39][40] If the comparison is limited to dog breeds of a similar size, then there are around 3–5 times as many Labradors registered in both countries as the next most popular breeds, the German shepherd dog and Golden retriever.[39][40]


They are the most popular breed of assistance dog in the United States, Australia, and many other countries,[41] as well as being widely used by police and other official bodies for their detection and working abilities. Approximately 60–70% of all guide dogs in the United States are Labradors.

### Temperament

[edit]

The Golden Retriever is considered an intelligent, gentle natured and very affectionate breed of dog.[3][8] As is typical with retriever breeds, the breed is generally calm and biddable, being very easy to train and extremely keen to please their master.[6][8] The breed is known to make excellent pets and family dogs, being generally extremely tolerant of children and keen to accompany any member of the family in a range of activities.[4] Due to their affable natures, the breed is often completely devoid of guarding instincts.[4] However, there have also been reports of some very aggressive Golden Retrievers in certain lineages. It has been suggested that these variations in aggression are partially caused by genetic factors.[14]

<title>French Bulldog</title>
<fragment>

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

between 1875 and 1917

1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia


## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

<title>French Bulldog</title>
<fragment>

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

[edit]

* ![1890](image)

1890
* ![1901, Maurice in New York City](image)

1901, Maurice in New York City
* ![1908, Anna Sacher](image)

1908, Anna Sacher
* ![1911, Ch. Stanmore Argus](image)

1911, Ch. Stanmore Argus
* ![1915](image)

1915
* ![between 1875 and 1917](image)

between 1875 and 1917
* ![1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia](image)

1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia


## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>
16. **^** "COMPARATIVE TABLES OF REGISTRATIONS FOR THE YEARS 2010 - 2019 INCLUSIVE" (PDF). *The Kennel Club UK*. Archived from the original (PDF) on 31 January 2020. Retrieved 18 May 2023.
17. **^** "Beloved and debated, French bulldog becomes top US dog breed". 15 March 2023. Retrieved 15 March 2023.
18. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** Club, American Kennel. "American Kennel Club - Dog Breed Standards" (PDF).
19. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "French Bulldog Dog Breed Information". *American Kennel Club*.
20. **^** American Kennel Club (11 November 2014). *The New Complete Dog Book: Official Breed Standards and All-New Profiles for 200 Breeds, 21st Edition*. i5 Publishing. p. 912. ISBN 9781621870913.
21. **^** "Introducing the French Bulldog". French Bulldog Club of England. Archived from the original on 6 August 2011. Retrieved 14 October 2011.

</fragment>
<fragment>
9. **^** [staff] (4 February 2022). Looking back: A Sacramento heiress and Murder on the French Bulldog Express. *Sacramento News & Review*. Archived 30 June 2022.
10. **^** "History of the FBDCA". *French Bull Dog Club of America*. Retrieved 2 January 2019.
11. **^** American Kennel Club 2013 Dog Registration Statistics Historical Comparisons & Notable Trends, The American Kennel Club, Retrieved 28 May 2014
12. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "AKC: Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2018". The American Kennel Club.
13. **^** "Top Twenty Breeds In Registration Order For The Years 2018 And 2019" (PDF). The Kennel Club (UK). Archived from the original (PDF) on 26 June 2020. Retrieved 23 June 2020.
14. **^** "Top 10 dog breeds in Australia 2017. Don't worry, they're all adorable". *NewsComAu*. Retrieved 12 April 2017.
15. **^** "UK Export Pedigrees Issued in 2019" (PDF). *The Kennel Club*. Archived from the original (PDF) on 31 January 2020. Retrieved 18 May 2023.

</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]


</fragment>
</document>

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

Performance dog sports

Main article: Canine Good Citizen

The AKC also offers the Canine Good Citizen program. This program tests dogs of any breed (including mixed breed) or type, registered or not, for basic behavior and temperament suitable for appearing in public and living at home.


Another AKC affiliate is AKC Reunite,[14] formerly AKC Companion Animal Recovery (AKC CAR), founded in 1995, which is North America's largest not-for-profit pet ID and recovery service.

<title>French Bulldog</title>
<fragment>

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

[edit]

* ![1890](image)

1890
* ![1901, Maurice in New York City](image)

1901, Maurice in New York City
* ![1908, Anna Sacher](image)

1908, Anna Sacher

1911, Ch. Stanmore Argus

1915

between 1875 and 1917
* ![1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia](image)

1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia


## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>

18. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** Club, American Kennel. "American Kennel Club - Dog Breed Standards" (PDF).
19. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "French Bulldog Dog Breed Information". *American Kennel Club*.
20. **^** American Kennel Club (11 November 2014). *The New Complete Dog Book: Official Breed Standards and All-New Profiles for 200 Breeds, 21st Edition*. i5 Publishing. p. 912. ISBN 9781621870913.
21. **^** "Introducing the French Bulldog". French Bulldog Club of England. Archived from the original on 6 August 2011. Retrieved 14 October 2011.

</fragment>
<fragment>
9. **^** [staff] (4 February 2022). Looking back: A Sacramento heiress and Murder on the French Bulldog Express. *Sacramento News & Review*. Archived 30 June 2022.

<fragment>

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]

<fragment>

According to the American Kennel Club, the French Bulldog has overtaken the Labrador as the most popular breed of dog. Before 2023, Labradors had held the top spot for 31 years.[17]



#### Historic photographs

1917 with Grand Duchesses Tatiana and Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia


## Description

[edit]

The American Kennel Club standard for the French Bulldog states that it should be muscular, with a soft and loose coat forming wrinkles.[7]

In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the Rockefellers and the J. P. Morgans. The American Kennel Club recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[5]: 8 In 2013, the American Kennel Club (AKC) ranked the French Bulldog as the 10th most popular breed in the United States, enjoying a sharp rise in popularity from 54th place a decade before, in 2003.[11] By 2014, they had moved up to become the ninth most popular AKC registered dog breed in the US and by the 2017 they were the fourth most popular.[12]
